newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Dissident Wang speaks out after fleeing from China.
newsitem.headline: Dissident Wang speaks out after fleeing from China.

text.p: Chinese dissident Wang Xizhe broke his silence on his last weekend's escape from China, telling supporters on Thursday that he had arrived safely in the United States.
Wang told Hong Kong media in a brief taped message that he was able to escape with the help of democracy activists in Hong Kong and the United States.

"I arrived in the U.S. safely with help from friends in Hong Kong, (Chinese) democracy activists in the U.S. and the U.S. government," he said, speaking in Cantonese, the Chinese dialect spoken in Hong Kong and southern China.
Wang arrived in San Francisco on October 15 after flying halfway round the world from Hong Kong in his dash to asylum, his wife said on Wednesday.
Suy Jiang said her husband left the British colony on Monday, flying via France and Russia before arriving in San Francisco.

The 46-year-old dissident said he was forced to leave China, even though he did not want to go. "I never wanted to leave the country, but the situation was very urgent and was not under my control," he said.
Wang said he would have been arrested had he delayed his departure from the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou.

Wang fled to Hong Kong from his home in southern China's Guangdong province last weekend, just days after authorities in Beijing arrested fellow democracy activist Liu Xiaobo and packed him off to a labour camp for three years.
Wang and Liu sparked reprisals against China's few remaining dissidents last month when they demanded the impeachment of President Jiang Zemin for violating the constitution.
However, Wang said in his message he might return to China, denying that he planned to remain permanently in the U.S.
"I don't believe I am on a road of no return," he said. "If I want to return to China, I can still do so."
"The most the government can do is to throw me in jail, but there is no reason that I can't return home," he added.
A spokesman for the San Francisco-based Alliance for a Democratic China has said Wang would speak publicly about his escape from China at a news conference in the city on Monday.
Su Jiang said earlier Wang had not decided what he was going to do in the United States.

Wang is the second dissident to have fled via Hong Kong this year. Liu Gang transited Hong Kong on his way to Boston in May after six years in prison for leading the 1989 student protests at Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
Washington has been generous in granting asylum to Beijing's political critics since the bloody 1989 military crackdown on protesters.
Scores, perhaps hundreds of Chinese dissidents have fled to the West since then through Hong Kong, activists in the territory say.
They were aided by a group called the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, according to the activists.
Activists in Hong Kong fear China will shut down the escape route after the British-ruled territory reverts to Beijing on July 1, 1997.
